justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I would have assessed as the recent price level of the underlying asset (likely a stock or ETF trading near 595–600). For the 1-day horizon, I anchored closely to the last observed price, applying only a small positive drift consistent with long-run average daily returns in equity markets, which are typically a fraction of a percent. The 1-week estimate of 599 reflects that same slight upward bias compounded over five trading days, while the 1-month estimate of 605 extends that drift further, incorporating the historical tendency for equity prices to trend modestly higher over time in the absence of specific negative catalysts.

The confidence interval widths were primarily driven by realized volatility scaling with the square root of time, which is the standard framework for thinking about price uncertainty. At the 1-day horizon, a roughly 1.3% half-width on either side of the point estimate reflects typical daily volatility for a broad market instrument or large-cap stock. By one week, the interval widens to roughly plus or minus 4.8%, and by one month it expands to approximately plus or minus 9.4%, all consistent with annualized volatility in the 25–30% range. I also incorporated a slight fat-tail adjustment, meaning I gave a bit more probability mass to extreme outcomes than a pure normal distribution would suggest, which is why the intervals are not perfectly symmetric around the point estimates.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes well outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden macro shock — such as an unexpected Federal Reserve policy shift, a geopolitical escalation, or a disappointing earnings release from a major index constituent — could easily produce a 5–10% move within a week. A broader market dislocation, liquidity event, or credit stress episode could push even further. On the upside, a surprisingly strong economic data print, a dovish policy pivot, or positive earnings surprises could drive a sharp rally. These tail events are precisely why the stated 90% confidence intervals, while already fairly wide at the 1-month horizon, could still be breached — historically, equity markets experience moves outside such bands more frequently than a simple Gaussian model would predict, perhaps 15–20% of the time rather than the nominal 10%.
